solution.concept_anchor: Simple majority amendments outside Article 368 scope
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because abolishing a state Legislative Council involves a resolution from the concerned state assembly, giving it the appearance of a complex, quasi-federal process that students associate with Article 368.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options involving any amendment governed by the special majority requirement of Article 368 — the question asks specifically about changes effected outside Article 368.
Identify that the abolition of Legislative Councils under Article 169 requires Parliament to act on a state assembly's resolution but uses ordinary legislative procedure — not Article 368.

Confirm that admission of new states (Article 2) and formation of new states (Article 3) are similarly outside Article 368, falling under ordinary legislation — but the option must match the specific provision tested.
Select option (b): quorum rules in Parliament are changed by ordinary legislation under Article 100, entirely outside Article 368 — this is the clearest example.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who have memorised that 'constitutional provisions need constitutional amendment' reflexively classify all changes to parliamentary procedure under Article 368. Quorum rules, salaries of MPs, and creation of new states sound weighty enough to demand special majority. The trap exploits this heuristic: the correct answer (quorum rules) feels too simple to be outside Article 368, causing students to over-complicate and pick a wrong option.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 is not the exclusive gateway for changing the Constitution. Parliament retains the power to alter numerous provisions through ordinary legislation passed by simple majority.

• Option (a) — Abolition of a state Legislative Council: This requires Parliament to pass legislation on the basis of a resolution by the concerned state assembly (Article 169). Though it involves the state assembly, it is ordinary legislation — not an Article 368 amendment. Incorrect as the 'only' example.
• Option (b) — Quorum rules in Parliament (Article 100): Correct. Quorum requirements can be altered by Parliament acting as an ordinary legislature. No special majority or state ratification needed.
• Option (c) — Election of the President: Amendment of the mode of election of the President requires special majority PLUS ratification by at least half the state legislatures — it is firmly within Article 368.
• Option (d) — Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131: The original jurisdiction is constitutional; changes to appellate jurisdiction under Article 138 can be by Parliament, but core jurisdiction provisions require Article 368 procedure.

Value Addition:
• Article 2 (admission of new states) and Article 3 (formation of new states) are amended by simple majority — classic UPSC test points.
• Salaries of constitutional functionaries including the President and judges are set/changed by ordinary Parliament legislation.
• The simple majority route requires Presidential assent but not the special majority or ratification that Article 368 demands.

solution.concept_anchor: Dual condition special majority under Article 368

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill passes in a House if supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting, even if this number falls short of a majority of the total membership of that House.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) requires BOTH conditions to be met simultaneously: two-thirds of members present and voting AND a majority of the total membership. Meeting only one condition is insufficient.

statement_analysis.statement: In the context of Article 368, 'total membership' refers to the full sanctioned strength of the House, not merely the number of members present on that day.
statement_analysis.reason: Total membership means the constitutionally sanctioned strength — 543 for Lok Sabha and 245 for Rajya Sabha — regardless of vacancies or absentees, making the effective threshold harder to clear.

statement_analysis.statement: No provision exists under the Constitution for resolving a deadlock between the two Houses on a Constitution Amendment Bill through a joint sitting.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 108, which provides for joint sittings, explicitly does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills. A deadlock results in the bill lapsing — Rajya Sabha holds equal power here.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because Statement 2 alone being correct is plausible for students who know the 'total membership' rule but incorrectly believe Statement 3 is false, assuming joint sittings can be convened for all parliamentary business.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 368(2) explicitly mandates both conditions — two-thirds present-and-voting AND majority of total membership — simultaneously. Statement 1 says one condition alone suffices. Eliminate options that mark Statement 1 as correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: 'Total membership' = full sanctioned strength, not those present. Statement 2 is correct. Retain options including Statement 2.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 108 (joint sitting) does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills — confirmed by the constitutional text. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect — this matches option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the confusion between the two conditions of the special majority. Many students know 'two-thirds' but forget the simultaneous 'majority of total membership' requirement, leading them to mark Statement 1 as correct. Statement 3 is the secondary trap — students familiar with joint sittings from Money Bill discussions sometimes assume the same mechanism applies to Constitution Amendment Bills.
solution.final_explanation:
The special majority for constitutional amendments under Article 368 is uniquely demanding — it imposes a dual threshold that must be cleared in the same vote.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Both conditions must be satisfied together. If only 300 of 543 Lok Sabha members are present, two-thirds of 300 = 200 votes. But the majority of total membership requires at least 272 votes. Since 200 < 272, the bill would fail even if all 300 present voted in favour.
• Statement 2 — Correct: 'Total membership' anchors the threshold to the sanctioned strength, preventing a depleted House from easily amending the Constitution on a low-attendance day.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Article 108 excludes Constitution Amendment Bills. This gives Rajya Sabha genuine co-equal power — unlike Money Bills where Lok Sabha prevails, or ordinary bills where joint sitting can override Rajya Sabha.

Value Addition:
• For ordinary special majority (e.g., removal of judges under Article 124), only two-thirds present and voting suffices — the total membership condition does not apply.
• Rajya Sabha's equal veto on constitutional amendments is one of its most significant constitutional powers.
• Currently, Rajya Sabha has 245 members — a valid amendment needs at least 163 votes (two-thirds of 245) AND at least 123 (majority of 245).

solution.concept_anchor: State ratification under Article 368 proviso — scope and limits

statement_analysis.statement: State Legislatures must ratify a Constitution Amendment Bill with a special majority — the same two-thirds threshold that applies to Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution requires ratification by at least half the state legislatures, but only by a simple majority within each ratifying legislature — no special majority is prescribed for state legislatures.

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill requiring state ratification under the Article 368 proviso must be ratified within a constitutionally prescribed time limit.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike some federal constitutions, Indian Constitution prescribes no time limit for state ratification. States may ratify at any point after Parliament passes the bill.

statement_analysis.statement: State Legislatures possess an independent power to initiate constitutional amendment proposals and forward them to Parliament for consideration.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) vests the power to initiate amendment bills exclusively in either House of Parliament. State legislatures can only ratify certain amendments — they cannot initiate them.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) ('all three incorrect') is actually the correct answer here, but students who partially recall that states play a ratification role often assume at least one statement must be correct, gravitating toward options (b) or (c).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: States ratify by simple majority — no special majority is required of state legislatures. Statement 1 incorrectly imposes the parliamentary special majority on state ratification. Mark as incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: The Indian Constitution, unlike the US Constitution's Article V process, sets no time limit for state ratification. Statement 2 is false. Mark as incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Article 368(2) says the amendment process begins with a bill introduced in either House of Parliament. States have no power to initiate. Statement 3 is false.

All three statements are incorrect — the question asks which are NOT correct, so all three qualify. The correct option is (d), but since the format here maps to option labels, option (a) in the presented options correctly captures 1 and 2 only — re-check stem options. The answer maps to the option that captures all three as incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits confusion between Parliament's special majority and states' ratification threshold. Students who know states must ratify may over-generalise the special majority requirement. Statement 2 exploits comparison with other constitutional systems. Statement 3 exploits confusion with the US model where states can call a constitutional convention — India's constitutional design gives states no such initiating power.
solution.final_explanation:
The ratification requirement for certain constitutional amendments under Article 368's proviso is frequently misunderstood in its scope and mechanics.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: State legislatures ratify by a simple majority of members present and voting — the Constitution imposes no special majority on them. Only Parliament must clear the two-conditions threshold.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No time limit is prescribed anywhere in Article 368 for state ratification. This contrasts with some other federal systems and is a consistent MCQ trap.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The exclusive power to initiate constitutional amendments rests with Parliament — specifically, either House. State legislatures can only pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate (as in Article 252), but even that is not initiation of an amendment bill.

Value Addition:
• Provisions requiring state ratification include: election of President, extent of executive and legislative power of Union and States, Supreme Court, High Courts, representation in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.
• In the USA, three-fourths of states must ratify most constitutional amendments — India's requirement (half, simple majority) is considerably less demanding.
• Once a state legislature has ratified, there is no explicit constitutional provision allowing it to withdraw that ratification — an untested grey area.

solution.concept_anchor: Evolution of Article 13 vs Article 368 jurisprudence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Golak Nath before Shankari Prasad, which tempts students who confuse the two cases as part of the same era without recalling the specific decades involved.
elimination_logic: Shankari Prasad was decided in 1951 — the earliest of the three landmark cases on this question. It must come first.
Golak Nath was decided in 1967 — it overruled Shankari Prasad, so it necessarily comes second.
Kesavananda Bharati was decided in 1973 — it overruled Golak Nath, placing it third.

The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's legislative response to Golak Nath — it falls between Golak Nath (1967) and Kesavananda (1973), confirming the sequence: Shankari Prasad → Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda Bharati. This matches option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here is the 24th Amendment's placement. Students who know the three landmark cases may not recall that the 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's direct legislative reaction to Golak Nath (1967) and preceded Kesavananda Bharati (1973). Placing the Amendment after Kesavananda — as option (c) does — is the classic error for a student who recalls events by rough era rather than precise year.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the Article 13 versus Article 368 conflict is one of the most important judicial timelines in Indian constitutional law.

Correct sequence: Shankari Prasad (1951) → Golak Nath (1967) → 24th Amendment (1971) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

• Shankari Prasad (1951): The Supreme Court held that constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13 — Parliament could curtail Fundamental Rights.
• Golak Nath (1967): The Supreme Court reversed course — amendments ARE 'law' under Article 13, and Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights. This left Parliament in crisis.
• 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament struck back by explicitly affirming its power to amend any part of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights and making Presidential assent mandatory.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973): The 13-judge bench overruled Golak Nath — amendments are not 'law' under Article 13, but the Basic Structure doctrine now limits amending power.

Value Addition:
• The 25th Amendment (1971) followed the 24th — it inserted Article 31C to protect DPSP-implementing laws from FR challenge.
• Kesavananda was decided on April 24, 1973 — this date is the Prospective Overruling cut-off recognised in Waman Rao (1981).
• The 24th Amendment also made it mandatory for the President to give assent to Constitution Amendment Bills.

solution.concept_anchor: Mandatory Presidential assent to Constitution Amendment Bills
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the most tempting incorrect answer because both A and R are factually correct; the trap is in believing that the 24th Amendment's purpose (asserting Parliament's power over FRs) causally explains why the President must give assent, when the actual causal chain is different — the mandatory assent rule was a specific procedural reform, not a derivation from Parliament's constituent power.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes. After the 24th Amendment, Article 368(2) proviso explicitly states the President 'shall give his assent' — the President has no discretionary power over Constitution Amendment Bills.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Yes. The 24th Amendment was indeed Parliament's legislative response to the Golak Nath judgment, affirming Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? No. The mandatory assent rule addresses a separate procedural concern — preventing Presidential veto over constitutional amendments. The reason Parliament affirmed its amending power (Golak Nath response) is a different objective from why the President's discretion was removed. R is a correct fact but not the causal explanation of A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic assertion-reason trap where both facts are correct but causally unconnected. A student who knows both facts but does not pause to test causality will jump to option (a). The 24th Amendment did multiple things simultaneously — affirming Parliament's amending power AND making Presidential assent mandatory — but the reason for mandatory assent is to prevent executive interference in the constituent process, not a consequence of overcoming the Golak Nath restriction. Separating the two distinct purposes of the same amendment is the key reasoning step.
solution.final_explanation:
The 24th Constitutional Amendment (1971) addressed two separate constitutional gaps simultaneously, which is why the assertion-reason trap here is particularly effective.

Assertion (A): Correct. Before the 24th Amendment, there was ambiguity about whether the President could withhold assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill — as with ordinary bills under Article 111. The 24th Amendment added the phrase 'shall give his assent' to Article 368(2), removing all Presidential discretion. The President cannot return the bill, exercise a pocket veto, or withhold assent.

Reason (R): Correct. The 24th Amendment was Parliament's direct response to Golak Nath (1967), which had held that Parliament could not abridge Fundamental Rights through constitutional amendments. The 24th Amendment amended both Article 13 and Article 368 to assert Parliament's power to amend any provision including Fundamental Rights.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The mandatory assent rule was introduced to prevent executive interference in Parliament's constituent power — its logic is about separation of powers between Parliament and the President, not about the Parliament-Judiciary conflict resolved through the Golak Nath response.

Value Addition:
• For ordinary bills under Article 111, the President has three options: assent, withhold assent, or return for reconsideration. None of these apply to Constitution Amendment Bills.
• The removal of Presidential discretion over Constitution Amendment Bills reflects Parliament's role as a constituent assembly — above its role as an ordinary legislature.
• The 24th Amendment is also responsible for making Presidential assent mandatory for Money Bills — a distinct but related reform.

solution.concept_anchor: Basic Structure restricts amendments not ordinary legislation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 'rights of citizens are diminished' sounds like a Fundamental Rights violation, leading students to think of Part III remedies rather than the Basic Structure doctrine — which applies specifically to constitutional amendments.
elimination_logic: Identify the nature of the impugned law: the Parliament passed a Constitutional Amendment Bill (Article 368 process), not ordinary legislation. The challenge must therefore be evaluated under the Basic Structure doctrine, not Article 13 directly.

The Basic Structure doctrine applies specifically to constitutional amendments — ordinary legislation is tested under Part III (Articles 13, 14, 19, 21 etc.) directly without invoking Basic Structure.

The principle that courts can strike down constitutional amendments for violating Basic Structure was established in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980) and the NJAC judgment (2015).

Option (c) correctly states the applicable principle: courts can review constitutional amendments but only on the ground that they abrogate or damage the Basic Structure — not on the ground of policy wisdom or that citizens' rights are merely 'diminished'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to make students choose between an Article 13 challenge (ordinary FR violation) and a Basic Structure challenge. Students who know Basic Structure broadly but have not internalised that it applies exclusively to constitutional amendments — not ordinary legislation — may conflate the two standards. Option (b) exploits the natural instinct to reach for fundamental rights violations when a law diminishes citizens' rights, even though that remedy applies only to ordinary legislation challenged under Article 13.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario maps directly to the foundational principle established in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and refined in Minerva Mills (1980).

Applicable principle: When Parliament amends the Constitution under Article 368, the Supreme Court can judicially review that amendment — but the standard of review is whether the amendment abrogates or destroys the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Courts cannot examine the policy wisdom behind the amendment.

Mapping to the scenario: The amendment in question restructures the federal division of powers between the Union and states — a core element of Basic Structure. The appropriate legal challenge is that it damages the federal character of the Constitution, which is a recognised Basic Structure element.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Parliament does not need Supreme Court approval before passing a constitutional amendment. Judicial review is post-facto.
• Option (b): Incorrect — 'Diminution of citizens' rights' invokes Article 13, which applies to ordinary legislation, not to constitutional amendments (post-Kesavananda settlement).
• Option (c): Correct — The Supreme Court can examine whether the amendment abrogates a Basic Structure element, and federalism is explicitly recognised as such.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Basic Structure scrutiny does not require state legislatures to have been bypassed; it applies even when Article 368's procedure is perfectly followed, as demonstrated in the NJAC case (2015).

Value Addition:
• The NJAC judgment (2015) demonstrated that even a constitutionally valid procedure (special majority + state ratification) cannot save an amendment that violates Basic Structure.
• Federalism as Basic Structure was confirmed in SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994).
• Courts examine 'abrogation or destruction' — not mere modification — of Basic Structure elements.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional amendments paired with their primary outcomes
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) pairs the 42nd Amendment with 'judicial review made non-justiciable', which is partially true but conflates the amendment's objective with its ultimate fate — the key fact is that Articles 368(4) and (5) were struck down in Minerva Mills, not that the amendment merely 'expanded DPSP primacy'.
elimination_logic: The 24th Amendment (1971) is firmly associated with affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution including FRs and making Presidential assent mandatory — this matches entry 2 (affirming constituent power and mandatory assent).
The 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C, shielding DPSP-implementing laws (Articles 39b/c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 — this matches entry 3.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to make constitutional amendments non-justiciable by inserting Articles 368(4) and (5) — this matches entry 4; these clauses were later struck down in Minerva Mills.

The 44th Amendment (1978) abolished the Fundamental Right to Property (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) and moved it to Article 300A as a constitutional right — this matches entry 1. Confirming: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 — but checking the options, (b) gives A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3... Re-evaluate using the table as presented.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap pairs the 42nd and 25th Amendments. Both relate to DPSP primacy — the 25th Amendment inserted Article 31C (shielding specific DPSPs from FR challenge), while the 42nd Amendment later expanded Article 31C's scope to all DPSPs. Students who know 'DPSP primacy = 25th Amendment' may over-confidently match the 42nd Amendment with an unrelated entry, missing the non-justiciability of amendments as the 42nd Amendment's defining (and ultimately struck-down) feature.
solution.final_explanation:
These four amendments represent Parliament's evolving legislative responses to judicial rulings over 1971–1978.

Correct pairings:
• 44th Amendment (1978) ↔ Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights: Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 were deleted; property became a constitutional right under Article 300A — not enforceable under Article 32.
• 24th Amendment (1971) ↔ Parliament's constituent power affirmed, Presidential assent made mandatory: Direct response to Golak Nath; amended both Article 13 and Article 368.
• 25th Amendment (1971) ↔ Article 31C inserted (DPSP-implementing laws protected from FR challenge): Protected laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
• 42nd Amendment (1976) ↔ Articles 368(4) and (5) inserted to make amendments non-justiciable: Struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) — Parliament cannot give itself unlimited amending power.

Trap pairings to avoid: Do not pair the 42nd Amendment with 'DPSP primacy' alone — that belongs to the 25th. The 42nd Amendment's constitutional signature is the (ultimately failed) attempt to oust judicial review over amendments.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd Amendment is sometimes called the 'Mini Constitution' for its sweeping scope — it amended over 50 provisions.
• Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Articles 368(4) and (5) but left other parts of the 42nd Amendment intact.
• The 44th Amendment also restored certain freedoms diluted by the Emergency — including restoring Article 19 protections during external emergency.

solution.concept_anchor: 9th Schedule immunity — post-1973 Kesavananda cut-off

statement_analysis.statement: All laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, regardless of when they were inserted, are immune from judicial review for violation of Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: In IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a 9-judge bench held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) can be judicially reviewed if they violate the Basic Structure or essential Fundamental Rights — the blanket immunity argument was rejected.

statement_analysis.statement: The doctrine of Prospective Overruling, first applied in Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, means that the new constitutional rule announced therein applied only to future constitutional amendments and not to those already enacted.
statement_analysis.reason: Golak Nath (1967) introduced Prospective Overruling into Indian jurisprudence — the court held that its new rule (amendments cannot abridge FRs) would apply prospectively, protecting all past amendments from challenge on that ground.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) ('both correct') tempts students who broadly know that 9th Schedule laws enjoy special protection and assume Statement 1 captures this immunity accurately, without recalling the IR Coelho cut-off date.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: IR Coelho (2007) specifically removed blanket immunity for post-April 24, 1973 insertions into the 9th Schedule. Statement 1 says 'regardless of when inserted' — this is false. Mark Statement 1 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Golak Nath (1967) is indeed the origin of Prospective Overruling in Indian constitutional law — the rule applied only to future amendments. Statement 2 is factually correct.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 1 exploits the broad popular knowledge that 'Ninth Schedule laws are immune from fundamental rights challenge.' This was true as an absolute rule before IR Coelho (2007) established the April 24, 1973 cut-off. Students who learned about the 9th Schedule without studying IR Coelho will confidently mark Statement 1 as correct. The date-specific nuance — only pre-Kesavananda insertions retain full immunity — is precisely the kind of precision UPSC rewards.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule's immunity from judicial review has been progressively qualified over five decades.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 9th Schedule was created by the 1st Amendment (1951) originally to protect land reform laws from Article 19(1)(f) challenge. For decades, it provided blanket immunity. IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) changed this — a 9-judge constitution bench ruled that post-April 24, 1973 insertions can be reviewed if they damage the Basic Structure or violate the essential core of Fundamental Rights. Currently 284 laws are in the Schedule; those inserted after 1973 now face potential judicial scrutiny.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Golak Nath (1967) introduced Prospective Overruling — the court acknowledged that striking down earlier amendments would cause constitutional chaos. The new rule (amendments = 'law' under Article 13) therefore applied only prospectively, shielding pre-1967 amendments from challenge on that ground. Kesavananda Bharati later overruled Golak Nath but used April 24, 1973 as its own prospective cut-off, recognised in Waman Rao (1981).

Value Addition:
• April 24, 1973 is one of the most important dates in Indian constitutional law — the Kesavananda Bharati judgment date.
• Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981) specifically held that amendments to the 9th Schedule made before April 24, 1973 cannot be challenged for Basic Structure violations.
• IR Coelho is the most recent and authoritative pronouncement on 9th Schedule immunity.

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — Articles 368(4) and (5) struck down
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) naming the Kesavananda Bharati case is the strongest distractor because students associate the Basic Structure doctrine primarily with that case and may not recall that it was Minerva Mills that specifically struck down the textual additions to Article 368.
elimination_logic: The question asks which case struck down Articles 368(4) and (5) — these were inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) to make amendments immune from judicial challenge.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the Basic Structure doctrine but predates the 42nd Amendment — it could not have struck down provisions inserted after it was decided.
Golak Nath (1967) and Shankari Prasad (1951) are even earlier — neither could address 42nd Amendment provisions.
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) specifically and explicitly struck down Articles 368(4) and (5) — the correct answer is option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes Kesavananda Bharati for Minerva Mills. Since Kesavananda is the more famous case — and the source of the Basic Structure doctrine itself — students naturally associate all Basic Structure enforcement with it. The critical distinction is that Kesavananda (1973) preceded the 42nd Amendment (1976), which inserted Articles 368(4) and (5). Only Minerva Mills (1980) could — and did — strike down those specific provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) was Parliament's most aggressive attempt to insulate constitutional amendments from judicial review. It inserted Articles 368(4) and (5), declaring that no constitutional amendment could be called in question in any court and that Parliament's constituent power was unlimited.

• Option (a) — Shankari Prasad (1951): Incorrect. This case held that amendments are not 'law' under Article 13 — it predates the 42nd Amendment by 25 years.
• Option (b) — Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Incorrect. Kesavananda established the Basic Structure doctrine but was decided in 1973 — three years before the 42nd Amendment inserted Articles 368(4) and (5).
• Option (c) — Golak Nath (1967): Incorrect. Golak Nath dealt with whether amendments could abridge FRs — entirely different from the non-justiciability provisions.
• Option (d) — Minerva Mills (1980): Correct. The Supreme Court held that an unlimited amending power would itself be unconstitutional — the power to amend cannot become a power to destroy. Judicial review and the harmony between FRs and DPSPs were confirmed as Basic Structure elements.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills is the only case where the Supreme Court struck down explicit text added to Article 368 itself.
• The Minerva Mills bench also clarified that Article 31C, as expanded by the 42nd Amendment to cover all DPSPs, was unconstitutional.
• The principle 'Parliament is the creature of the Constitution, not its master' flows directly from Minerva Mills.

solution.concept_anchor: Judicially recognised Basic Structure elements
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Free and fair elections' as a Basic Structure element is less well-known and students may doubt it, making them pick (c) as the odd one out rather than the correct answer (b).
elimination_logic: Identify which of the four has been explicitly recognised as a Basic Structure element in landmark judgments: Supremacy of the Constitution, Separation of Powers, Free and Fair Elections, and Uniform Civil Code.

Supremacy of the Constitution — affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati. Separation of Powers — affirmed in Kesavananda and subsequent cases. Free and Fair Elections — affirmed in cases involving election law (Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975). All three are recognised Basic Structure elements.
Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) is a Directive Principle — a constitutional aspiration, not a justiciable right, and has never been recognised as a Basic Structure element by any Supreme Court bench.
Uniform Civil Code is the odd one out — it is a DPSP, not a judicially recognised element of the Basic Structure. Correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap works because Uniform Civil Code sounds like a constitutional principle that might qualify for Basic Structure status — it is in the Constitution (Article 44), it is debated in major political and judicial forums, and its implementation touches constitutional identity. A student who has not specifically studied which elements have been judicially confirmed as Basic Structure may include the UCC in the list, particularly when 'Free and Fair Elections' (the less familiar genuine element) is also present as a more suspicious-looking option.
solution.final_explanation:
The Basic Structure doctrine's element list is judicially assembled across multiple cases — it is neither exhaustive nor codified.

• Option (a) — Supremacy of the Constitution: Genuine Basic Structure element, identified in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
• Option (b) — Uniform Civil Code: The odd one out. Article 44 places UCC in the DPSP chapter as a directive to the state — it is aspirational and non-justiciable. No Supreme Court bench has recognised UCC as a Basic Structure element. Its inclusion here is the trap.
• Option (c) — Free and Fair Elections: Genuine Basic Structure element. Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and subsequent cases confirm this. Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to eliminate free and fair elections.
• Option (d) — Separation of Powers: Genuine Basic Structure element identified in Kesavananda Bharati and reinforced in Indira Gandhi case.

Value Addition:
• Other confirmed Basic Structure elements include: Republican and Democratic form of government, secular character, federal character, judicial review, rule of law, parliamentary system, and unity and integrity of India.
• The Basic Structure list is open-ended — courts can recognise new elements. 'Right to vote' was debated in PUCL v. Union of India.
• DPSPs, including UCC, cannot be Basic Structure elements — they are directive and non-justiciable.

solution.concept_anchor: NJAC judgment — 99th Amendment struck down despite procedural compliance

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment establishing the National Judicial Appointments Commission on the ground that it violated the Basic Structure of the Constitution by compromising the independence of the judiciary.
statement_analysis.reason: In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015), a 5-judge bench (4:1 majority) struck down the 99th Amendment, holding that the independence of judiciary and the primacy of judiciary in appointments are Basic Structure elements violated by the NJAC's composition giving a decisive role to the executive.

statement_analysis.statement: The 99th Amendment was declared unconstitutional primarily because it was passed without the required ratification by at least half the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The 99th Amendment was in fact ratified by more than half the state legislatures — the constitutional procedure under Article 368 was fully complied with. The amendment was struck down purely on Basic Structure grounds, demonstrating that procedural compliance does not save an amendment that violates the Basic Structure.

statement_analysis.statement: The NJAC judgment reaffirmed that judicial review of constitutional amendments on Basic Structure grounds is itself an element of the Basic Structure.
statement_analysis.reason: The NJAC judgment, by exercising the power to strike down a constitutionally passed amendment, necessarily reaffirmed what Kesavananda and Minerva Mills had established — that judicial review of amendments is itself protected as Basic Structure and cannot be removed by Parliament.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) (Statements 1 and 3 only) is the correct answer, but students who believe Statement 2 is also correct (confusing procedural non-compliance with the actual ground of challenge) will drift toward option (d) including all three.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2 first — it is the decisive trap. The 99th Amendment WAS ratified by more than half the state legislatures; procedural compliance was full. The challenge was purely substantive (Basic Structure). Mark Statement 2 as incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 1: The NJAC judgment's holding on independence of judiciary as Basic Structure is the cornerstone of the case — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The very act of striking down a constitutionally passed amendment reaffirms judicial review as Basic Structure — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — matches option (a) if options list '1 and 3 only' as (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the deliberate partial-truth trap. Many students know the NJAC amendment was challenged and struck down but conflate the ground of challenge with procedural defects. The powerful teaching point — and the UPSC-worthy nuance — is that the 99th Amendment followed every procedural step of Article 368 perfectly (special majority in both Houses AND ratification by more than half the states) and was STILL struck down. This demonstrates that formal constitutional compliance cannot override the Basic Structure limitation.
solution.final_explanation:
The NJAC judgment (2015) is the most significant recent application of the Basic Structure doctrine and illustrates its supreme position above Article 368's procedural requirements.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Supreme Court (4:1 majority) held that judicial independence and the primacy of the judiciary in its own appointments are Basic Structure elements. The NJAC, by giving two eminent persons and the Law Minister a role in appointments, diluted judicial primacy sufficiently to damage this element.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This is the core trap. The 99th Amendment was ratified by more than half the state legislatures — Jammu & Kashmir, Maharashtra, and over 16 other state assemblies passed it. The challenge was entirely on substantive Basic Structure grounds, not procedural.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The court's exercise of power to invalidate the amendment is itself an act of judicial review over a constitutional amendment — reaffirming that this power (established in Kesavananda, reinforced in Minerva Mills) is beyond Parliament's reach.

Value Addition:
• The lone dissent in NJAC (4:1) was by Justice Chelameswar, who favoured striking down only the offending parts while retaining the NJAC framework.
• Post-NJAC, the collegium system remains operative — no alternative has been enacted.
• The NJAC case is cited as the most dramatic demonstration that procedural correctness under Article 368 is necessary but not sufficient to sustain a constitutional amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: Procedural rules specific to Constitution Amendment Bills

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2) explicitly states that an amendment may be initiated in either House — unlike Money Bills, which can only be introduced in Lok Sabha.

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced only by a Minister of the Union Cabinet, not by a private member of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 imposes no restriction on who may introduce an amendment bill. Any member of Parliament — minister or private member — may introduce a Constitution Amendment Bill.

statement_analysis.statement: If the Rajya Sabha passes a Constitution Amendment Bill with amendments unacceptable to Lok Sabha, a joint sitting of both Houses may be convened to resolve the deadlock.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 108, which provides for joint sittings, does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills. A deadlock between the Houses results in the bill lapsing — there is no joint sitting mechanism for constitutional amendments.

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill, after being passed by both Houses, must be presented to the President, who is constitutionally obligated to give assent.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(2), as amended by the 24th Amendment, provides that the bill 'shall be presented to the President for assent' and the President 'shall give his assent thereto' — Presidential discretion has been completely removed.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 'Only two' is the trap for students who correctly reject Statement 3 (no joint sitting) but are misled by Statement 2 into thinking only ministers can introduce — since most significant bills are in practice introduced by ministers, the 'private member' possibility is frequently overlooked.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Either House can initiate — correct. Count 1.
Statement 2: Private members CAN introduce Constitution Amendment Bills — Statement 2 is false. Do not count.
Statement 3: No joint sitting mechanism exists for Constitution Amendment Bills under Article 108 — Statement 3 is false. Do not count.
Statement 4: Presidential assent is mandatory post-24th Amendment — correct. Count 2. Total correct = 2, so answer is option (b) 'Only two'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates the normal legislative practice (most bills introduced by ministers) with a constitutional rule. In practice, privately-introduced Constitution Amendment Bills are rare but constitutionally permissible — Article 368 contains no restriction. Students who derive constitutional rules from observed practice rather than textual reading will mark Statement 2 as correct, inflating the count to three and selecting option (c) incorrectly.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural rules governing Constitution Amendment Bills differ from those for ordinary legislation in several important respects.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Either House may originate a Constitution Amendment Bill. This contrasts with Money Bills (Lok Sabha only) and gives Rajya Sabha equal initiating power.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No constitutional provision restricts introduction to ministers. Private member Constitution Amendment Bills have been introduced historically, though rarely passed. The restriction to ministers exists in practice, not in constitutional text.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 108 (joint sitting) explicitly excludes Constitution Amendment Bills. If the two Houses cannot agree, the bill lapses. This gives Rajya Sabha a genuine absolute veto on constitutional amendments — unlike Money Bills or ordinary legislation.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Post-24th Amendment, Article 368(2) makes Presidential assent mandatory. The President has no power to return, withhold, or pocket-veto a Constitution Amendment Bill.

Only Statements 1 and 4 are correct — 'Only two.'

Value Addition:
• The distinction between introduction rules for Money Bills (Lok Sabha only), ordinary bills (either House), and Constitution Amendment Bills (either House) is a recurring UPSC test point.
• Rajya Sabha's veto on constitutional amendments is its strongest constitutional power — stronger than its role in ordinary legislation.
• A private member introduced the Constitution (Amendment) Bill that ultimately became the Right to Education Amendment — though government versions usually prevail.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th Amendment — Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights
solution.strong_distractor: a — '42nd Amendment — Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights' is the strongest distractor because the 42nd Amendment (1976, Emergency era) is associated with sweeping changes to the Constitution, and students who know the Right to Property was removed during the Emergency period but forget the precise amendment number will select (a).
elimination_logic: The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights — identify the correct amendment number. It was moved to Article 300A as a constitutional right, not a fundamental right.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) was an Emergency-era amendment known for expanding DPSP primacy, making amendments non-justiciable, and other sweeping changes — it did NOT remove the Right to Property.

The 44th Amendment (1978), enacted by the Janata government post-Emergency, deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 (fundamental right to property) and inserted Article 300A (constitutional right to property).
The pair '44th Amendment — Right to Property relocated from FR list to Article 300A' is correctly matched — this is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap between the 42nd and 44th Amendments is one of the most reliably tested traps in UPSC Polity. Both amendments dealt with significant changes to fundamental rights architecture. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is associated with the Emergency and 'mini constitution' notoriety, making students assume it contains the property rights change. In fact, it was the 44th Amendment (1978) by the Janata government — often remembered as the post-Emergency corrective amendment — that abolished property as a Fundamental Right.
solution.final_explanation:
The removal of the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights chapter is one of the most significant structural changes to Part III of the Constitution.

• Option (a) — 42nd Amendment, Right to Property removed: Incorrect. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is the 'mini constitution' of the Emergency era — it expanded DPSP primacy (Art.31C), made amendments non-justiciable, and extended Lok Sabha's term. It did not remove property rights.
• Option (b) — 44th Amendment, Right to Property relocated: Correct. The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted Article 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) and Article 31 (compulsory acquisition) from the Fundamental Rights chapter, inserting Article 300A — which protects property but is not enforceable under Article 32.
• Option (c) — 25th Amendment, Article 31C inserted: Correct as stated but this describes Article 31C's insertion, not the removal of property as a fundamental right — wrong pair as presented.
• Option (d) — 43rd Amendment, property rights changes: Incorrect. The 43rd Amendment (1977) reversed certain Emergency changes but did not deal specifically with the property rights relocation.

Value Addition:
• Post-44th Amendment, property is a constitutional right under Article 300A — violation is remediable through High Courts under Article 226 but NOT directly under Article 32.
• The Right to Property as a Fundamental Right was controversial from the start — it was the source of the 1st Amendment (1951) and much of the early property-DPSP conflict.
• Article 300A requires that no person shall be deprived of their property save by authority of law — but does not guarantee compensation.

solution.concept_anchor: Amending power as limited constituent power — not sovereign power
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Basic Structure limits amending power AND that this flows from Kesavananda may conclude R correctly explains A, not pausing to test whether the causal direction stated in R is accurate or whether there is a more precise causal link.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes. Post-Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980), it is settled that Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is a limited constituent power — not an unlimited sovereign power.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Yes. It is factually accurate that the Basic Structure doctrine operates as an implied limitation on Article 368 — courts can strike down amendments that abrogate Basic Structure.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Partially — but not precisely. R states the consequence (Basic Structure as limitation) rather than the causal basis. The precise reason A is correct is that Article 368 confers a 'power to amend' — not a power to replace, abrogate, or destroy the Constitution — which inherently implies limits. The Basic Structure doctrine is the judicial recognition of this inherent limit, not the cause of it. R and A describe the same phenomenon from different angles — R is correct but is not the causal explanation of A, it is a restatement of the same principle.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT causally explain A → correct option is (b). Re-check: the explanation above leads to (b), which must match correct_option. Set correct_option to 'b'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question tests whether students can distinguish between a causal explanation and a restatement of the same principle. Both A and R are factually true and conceptually connected — Parliament's amending power is limited (A), and the Basic Structure doctrine is that limitation (R). The trap is that R does not explain WHY A is true — it describes the same phenomenon from a different angle. The 'cause' of A is the inherent nature of constituent power as distinct from sovereign power (a power to amend is not the same as a power to destroy). R is an effect or expression of that limitation, not its cause.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between constituent power and sovereign power is fundamental to understanding the limits of Article 368.

Assertion (A): Correct. Parliament's power under Article 368 is a 'power to amend' — which inherently connotes change within an existing framework, not replacement or destruction of that framework. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) settled that this is a limited constituent power. Parliament is not a sovereign constituent assembly — it derives its power from the Constitution and cannot turn that power against the Constitution's identity.

Reason (R): Correct. The Basic Structure doctrine operates as a judicially implied limitation on Article 368. Courts can review and strike down constitutional amendments that damage the Basic Structure.

Causal relationship: R does NOT precisely explain A. A is true because of the inherent nature of 'amending power' — a word ('amend') that by its ordinary meaning implies modification within the existing structure, not replacement. R describes the judicial enforcement mechanism of this inherent limitation — it is the effect of the principle stated in A, not its cause. R and A describe linked but different aspects of the same constitutional truth.

Value Addition:
• The phrase 'amend by way of addition, variation or repeal' in Article 368(1) is significant — 'repeal' here means repeal of a provision, not repeal of the Constitution itself.
• Kesavananda's 13-judge bench remains the largest constitution bench ever assembled in the Supreme Court of India.
• The Basic Structure doctrine is unique to India — no other major democracy has an equivalent judicially enforced limitation on constitutional amendment power.

solution.concept_anchor: India vs USA state ratification — comparative federalism in amendment procedure
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that India requires 'half the states' ratification and the USA requires a 'supermajority' sometimes conflate the USA's three-fourths requirement with India's own procedure, marking (b) as correct.
elimination_logic: The question asks for an accurate statement comparing India's and the USA's constitutional amendment processes in terms of state participation.
Eliminate options claiming India requires state ratification for all amendments — only specific provisions listed in the Article 368 proviso require state ratification.
Eliminate options mischaracterising the USA requirement — the USA requires three-fourths of states (not two-thirds) to ratify most amendments under Article V.

The correct contrast is: India requires simple majority ratification by at least half the states (only for specific provisions), while the USA requires three-fourths of states — making the USA's federal participation requirement more demanding. This matches option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap here operates between two countries' amendment systems. Students who recall that 'USA requires state ratification' but mistake the fraction (two-thirds vs three-fourths) will eliminate option (d) as an 'overstatement.' The correct fact — USA requires three-fourths, India requires at least half — is a precise numerical distinction that separates well-prepared students from those who have only a rough comparative sense.
solution.final_explanation:
India's constitutional amendment procedure occupies a middle ground on the federal spectrum — more unitary than the USA but not purely parliamentary.

• Option (a): Incorrect. India does not require state ratification for all constitutional amendments — only those listed in the Article 368 proviso (election of President, federal division of powers, Supreme Court, High Courts, etc.).
• Option (b): Incorrect. When state ratification is required in India, state legislatures act by simple majority — not special majority. Only Parliament must satisfy the dual special majority condition.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The USA under Article V requires three-fourths of state legislatures (or ratifying conventions) to ratify constitutional amendments — not two-thirds. This is a common numerical error.
• Option (d): Correct. India requires ratification by at least half (simple majority within each state legislature) of states for specific provisions, while the USA requires three-fourths state ratification for most amendments — making the American process more demanding of state participation.

Value Addition:
• In the USA, states can also call for a Constitutional Convention if two-thirds of state legislatures demand it — no equivalent exists in India.
• India's limited state ratification requirement reflects its quasi-federal character — the Centre retains primacy in constitutional architecture.
• SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994) confirmed that federalism is a Basic Structure element, limiting how far the Centre can alter the federal balance even through Article 368.

solution.concept_anchor: Provisions changeable by ordinary legislation vs Article 368

statement_analysis.statement: The abolition of a state Legislative Council under Article 169 is effected by Parliament through ordinary legislation passed on the basis of a resolution by the concerned state assembly, without invoking Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 169 provides a specific procedure — Parliament can abolish (or create) a state Legislative Council by ordinary legislation if the concerned state assembly passes a resolution by special majority requesting it. This process falls outside Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: The Anti-Defection Law, added to the Constitution as the Tenth Schedule by the 52nd Amendment (1985), can only be amended through the Article 368 special majority procedure since it forms part of the constitutional text.
statement_analysis.reason: Since the Anti-Defection Law is part of the Constitution (added by the 52nd Amendment via Article 368 procedure), any amendment to it must also follow Article 368. Being a constitutional Schedule makes it subject to the Article 368 amendment route.

statement_analysis.statement: Delimitation of parliamentary constituencies is a constitutional matter and can therefore only be changed through the Article 368 amendment procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: Delimitation is governed by the Delimitation Act — ordinary parliamentary legislation. The constitutional provision (Articles 82 and 170) sets the framework, but the actual delimitation process is carried out through ordinary statute and the Delimitation Commission Act, not Article 368.

solution.strong_distractor: d — '1, 2 and 3' is the trap for students who assume that anything touching constitutional provisions must be amended via Article 368 — the conflation between 'constitutional subject matter' and 'Article 368 amendment route' is the central misconception tested here.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 3 first — delimitation is carried out through ordinary legislation (Delimitation Acts), not Article 368. The fact that it relates to parliamentary constituencies does not make the change a constitutional amendment. Mark Statement 3 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 1 — Article 169 is a self-contained provision establishing its own procedure (ordinary bill + state resolution). Confirm it operates outside Article 368. Mark Statement 1 correct.
Evaluate Statement 2 — the 10th Schedule was added by a constitutional amendment (52nd Amendment). Its modification requires Article 368. Mark Statement 2 correct.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — matches option (a) '1 and 2 only'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the conflation between 'constitutional subject matter' and 'the Article 368 procedure.' Delimitation of constituencies is constitutionally anchored (Articles 82, 170) — it appears constitutional. But the actual delimitation is done by ordinary legislation through the Delimitation Acts. Students who see 'constituency delimitation' and conclude 'Article 368 required' make the classic error of confusing the constitutional framework with the implementing mechanism.
solution.final_explanation:
The line between constitutional amendments and ordinary legislation is not always intuitive — constitutional subject matter can sometimes be adjusted through ordinary statute.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 169 carves out its own procedure for creating or abolishing state Legislative Councils. Parliament passes ordinary legislation after the state assembly passes a resolution by a special majority. No Article 368 special majority in Parliament is needed.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 10th Schedule (Anti-Defection Law), being part of the constitutional text added through the 52nd Amendment under Article 368, requires the Article 368 route for any amendment. Its constitutional status is determined by how it was inserted.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Delimitation is primarily a statutory exercise. The Constitution (Articles 82, 170) provides for delimitation after each census, but the Delimitation Acts enacted by Parliament as ordinary legislation create the Delimitation Commission and set out the process. Changing delimitation does not require Article 368.

Value Addition:
• Citizenship rules (Article 11) empower Parliament to legislate on citizenship by ordinary law — hence the Citizenship Act is ordinary legislation despite its constitutional backing.
• Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 138 can be expanded by Parliament through ordinary legislation.
• The criterion of 'how was it inserted' vs 'what does it deal with' is the most reliable test for whether Article 368 applies.

solution.concept_anchor: Standard of judicial review for constitutional amendments post-Kesavananda

statement_analysis.statement: After the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, the Supreme Court may strike down a constitutional amendment if it finds that the amendment's policy objective was unwise or contrary to the public interest.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court's jurisdiction over constitutional amendments is limited to examining whether the amendment abrogates or damages the Basic Structure — courts explicitly cannot examine the policy wisdom or the political motivations behind an amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: The standard of review applied to constitutional amendments under the Basic Structure doctrine requires courts to examine whether the amendment 'abrogates or damages' the Basic Structure, not merely whether it 'affects' or 'modifies' a Basic Structure element.
statement_analysis.reason: The threshold is high — mere modification or incidental effect on a Basic Structure element does not suffice to strike down an amendment. Courts look for fundamental damage or destruction of the element, not any change whatsoever.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both statements being correct is tempting for students who do not read Statement 1 carefully enough to catch the 'policy objective was unwise' language — confusing the scope of judicial power over legislation (where courts do sometimes examine reasonableness) with the more limited scope over constitutional amendments.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The language 'policy objective was unwise or contrary to public interest' is the key flag. Courts have repeatedly held they cannot examine the wisdom of constitutional amendments — only their constitutional validity vis-à-vis Basic Structure. Statement 1 is false.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 'abrogates or damages' standard is correctly stated — it is a higher threshold than 'affects' or 'modifies.' Minor changes to elements of Basic Structure do not automatically invalidate an amendment. Statement 2 is correct.

Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct → option (d). Re-check options: (c) 'Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct' — this is option (c) in the standard two-statement format used here. Correct option is (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is the scope-extension of judicial power over constitutional amendments. Students who know courts can 'review' constitutional amendments sometimes extend this to mean courts can also question policy wisdom — which is the standard applied to ordinary legislation under Articles 14 and 19 (arbitrariness, reasonableness). The critical distinction is that for ordinary legislation, courts apply proportionality and reasonableness review; for constitutional amendments, the ONLY ground is Basic Structure damage — policy wisdom is completely outside the court's remit.
solution.final_explanation:
Judicial review of constitutional amendments operates on a distinctly narrow standard compared to review of ordinary legislation.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Policy wisdom is entirely beyond judicial scrutiny for constitutional amendments. The Supreme Court has consistently held that it cannot evaluate whether the policy behind an amendment is wise, necessary, or beneficial. This restraint is part of the separation of powers between Parliament (as constituent assembly) and the judiciary. The court's role is limited to the constitutional validity question — does the amendment damage the Basic Structure?
• Statement 2 — Correct: The threshold for striking down a constitutional amendment under Basic Structure is 'abrogation or damage' — a high bar. An amendment that modifies the contours of a Basic Structure element without fundamentally undermining it may survive judicial scrutiny. This is why most constitutional amendments survive — only those that strike at the core identity of constitutional elements (like the NJAC amendment eliminating judicial primacy) are struck down.

Value Addition:
• This limited scope of review reflects the difference between judicial review (courts check constitutional validity) and judicial supervision of parliamentary policy (which courts cannot exercise over constituent acts).
• In the NJAC case (2015), the court did not question whether NJAC was a good policy — it asked only whether judicial primacy in appointments (a Basic Structure element) was abrogated.
• Ordinary legislation is reviewed for arbitrariness, proportionality, and reasonableness — standards inapplicable to constitutional amendments.

solution.concept_anchor: Provisions requiring state ratification under Article 368 proviso

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment to the provisions governing the election of the President of India — requires state ratification
statement_analysis.reason: The election of the President is explicitly listed in the Article 368 proviso as a provision requiring ratification by at least half the state legislatures.

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment to the provisions governing the salaries and allowances of Members of Parliament — requires state ratification
statement_analysis.reason: Salaries of MPs are altered by ordinary legislation (simple majority) — this falls entirely outside Article 368 and therefore requires no state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment to Article 368 itself — requires state ratification
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 itself is explicitly listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as one of the provisions that requires ratification by not less than half the state legislatures before the President can give assent.

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment to provisions relating to the representation of states in Parliament — requires state ratification
statement_analysis.reason: Representation of states in Parliament is among the provisions listed in the Article 368 proviso requiring state ratification — this is a federal provision protecting states' stake in the composition of Parliament.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify items 1, 3, and 4 as requiring ratification but mistakenly include item 2 (salaries of MPs), thinking that any change to Parliament's functioning requires a formal constitutional amendment with state participation.
elimination_logic: Item 1 (Election of President): Listed in Article 368 proviso — requires state ratification. Count 1.
Item 2 (Salaries of MPs): Ordinary legislation, completely outside Article 368. No state ratification. Do not count.
Item 3 (Article 368 itself): Explicitly listed in the proviso — requires state ratification. Count 2.

Item 4 (Representation of states in Parliament): Listed in proviso — requires state ratification. Count 3. Total = 3 provisions correctly matched as requiring state ratification → 'Only three' → option (c). But the question asks how many of the pairs correctly pair the provision with 'requires state ratification' — Items 1, 3, 4 are correct; Item 2 is not. That gives 3 correct pairings. Correct answer: option (c) 'Only three'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes MPs' salaries (ordinary legislation) for a genuine Article 368 proviso provision. Students who have a general sense that 'important constitutional matters need state ratification' may include salaries of high constitutional functionaries in the ratification-requiring category, especially since salaries of the President and judges are set differently. The distinction between salaries of MPs (ordinary statute) and structural constitutional provisions (Article 368 proviso) is exactly the kind of precision UPSC rewards.
solution.final_explanation:
The Article 368 proviso identifies specific provisions whose amendment triggers the state ratification requirement — this list is exhaustive and must be memorised precisely.

• Item 1 — Correct pair: Election of the President is in the proviso list. Any change to how the President is elected (e.g., changing the electoral college) requires at least half the states to ratify.
• Item 2 — Incorrect pair: MPs' salaries and allowances are set by ordinary legislation under Article 106. Parliament passes this as an ordinary bill — no special majority, no state ratification.
• Item 3 — Correct pair: Article 368 itself is self-referentially included in the ratification requirement — an amendment to the amending procedure needs states' concurrence, reflecting the fundamental nature of that provision.
• Item 4 — Correct pair: Representation of states in Parliament (composition of Rajya Sabha, state representation in Lok Sabha) is in the proviso — states have a direct stake in ensuring Parliament's composition cannot be changed unilaterally by the Centre.

Three pairs are correctly matched → 'Only three' → option (c).

Value Addition:
• Other proviso-listed provisions include: extent of executive and legislative power of Union and States, Supreme Court provisions, and High Courts provisions.
• The ratification requirement reflects the quasi-federal character of India — purely federal matters require state concurrence.
• State ratification requires a simple majority in each ratifying legislature — no minimum quorum or special voting rule is imposed.

Ninth Schedule and Constitutional Amendments: IR Coelho Case

solution.concept_anchor: IR Coelho — post-1973 Ninth Schedule additions reviewable
solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Laws in the Ninth Schedule inserted before Kesavananda Bharati can now be challenged for violating Basic Structure' is the mirror-image error — students who partially recall the IR Coelho rule may invert it, applying the scrutiny to pre-1973 insertions instead of post-1973 ones.
elimination_logic: Identify the correct rule from IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): the cut-off date is April 24, 1973 — the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.
Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule BEFORE April 24, 1973 retain blanket immunity — they cannot be challenged for Basic Structure or FR violations under the Waman Rao principle.
Laws inserted AFTER April 24, 1973 can now be judicially reviewed if they violate Basic Structure or the essential core of Fundamental Rights.
Option (b) correctly states this — post-Kesavananda insertions face judicial scrutiny while pre-Kesavananda insertions retain immunity.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap inverts the IR Coelho cut-off. Students who know 'IR Coelho changed 9th Schedule immunity' but have not precisely internalised which insertions lose immunity (post-1973) vs which retain it (pre-1973) will select the inverted option. This is a high-frequency UPSC trap because April 24, 1973 is a well-known date but its application (pre vs post immunity) requires precision that hurried reading misses.
solution.final_explanation:
IR Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) is the definitive judgment on the Ninth Schedule's relationship with the Basic Structure doctrine.

• Option (a): Incorrect — inverts the rule. Pre-Kesavananda insertions (before April 24, 1973) retain immunity under the Waman Rao principle. They cannot be challenged on Basic Structure grounds.
• Option (b): Correct. The 9-judge bench in IR Coelho held that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be subjected to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure or the essential core of Fundamental Rights. The court reasoned that the date of the Kesavananda judgment is the constitutional watershed — Parliament was on notice of Basic Structure after that date.
• Option (c): Incorrect — suggests all 9th Schedule laws face scrutiny regardless of insertion date. This overstates IR Coelho's holding.
• Option (d): Incorrect — the protection under Ninth Schedule immunity applies to FR challenges, not merely to Article 14 alone. The immunity (where it exists) is broader.

Value Addition:
• Currently 284 laws are in the Ninth Schedule — the original 13 from the 1st Amendment (1951) have grown significantly.
• Land reform laws placed in the 9th Schedule before 1973 remain fully protected.
• IR Coelho is a 9-judge bench decision — its authority is binding on all lower benches and cannot be overruled except by a larger bench.

(b) Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be judicially reviewed if they violate the Basic Structure or the essential core of Fundamental Rights, while those inserted before that date retain their immunity.
(c) All laws in the Ninth Schedule, regardless of when they were inserted, are now subject to judicial review for any violation of Part III of the Constitution.

Article 13 vs Article 368: The Law-Amendment Conflict

solution.concept_anchor: Shankari Prasad — amendment not 'law' under Article 13
solution.strong_distractor: b — Golak Nath is the distractor because it addressed the same Article 13 question but reached the opposite conclusion — students who remember the conflict but not which case held which position select (b).
elimination_logic: The question asks which case first held that a constitutional amendment is NOT 'law' under Article 13(2) — allowing Parliament to curtail Fundamental Rights.
Golak Nath (1967) held the OPPOSITE — that amendments ARE 'law' and cannot abridge FRs. Eliminate Golak Nath.
Kesavananda (1973) overruled Golak Nath but applied the Basic Structure limitation — it did not hold amendments are simply 'not law' without qualification. Eliminate Kesavananda.
Shankari Prasad (1951) is the first and direct answer — it held constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13. Correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap is between Shankari Prasad and Golak Nath — two cases that addressed the identical question and reached opposite conclusions. Students who associate 'Article 13 and constitutional amendments' with the Article 13/368 conflict may recall Golak Nath as the more famous case and select it without checking which case held which position. The precise chronology — Shankari Prasad first said amendments are NOT law; Golak Nath later said they ARE law — is the discriminating fact.
solution.final_explanation:
The question of whether a constitutional amendment is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) was first authoritatively addressed in 1951.

• Option (a) — Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951): Correct. This case arose when the 1st Amendment was challenged as abridging the Fundamental Right to property. The Supreme Court held that constitutional amendments under Article 368 are not 'law' within Article 13(2) — 'law' refers to ordinary legislation, not constituent acts. Parliament could, therefore, curtail Fundamental Rights through amendments.
• Option (b) — Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967): Incorrect for this blank. Golak Nath reached the opposite conclusion — amendments ARE 'law' under Article 13, overruling Shankari Prasad. It caused Parliament a constitutional crisis.
• Option (c) — Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): Incorrect. Kesavananda overruled Golak Nath and returned to the Shankari Prasad position (amendments not 'law' under Art.13) but added the Basic Structure limitation — a more nuanced position.
• Option (d) — Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Incorrect. Minerva Mills confirmed Kesavananda's Basic Structure doctrine but did not revisit the Article 13 question.

Value Addition:
• Article 368(3), inserted by the 24th Amendment, explicitly states that nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under Article 368 — legislatively codifying the Kesavananda/Shankari Prasad position.
• The 1st Amendment (1951) is what triggered Shankari Prasad — it added the 9th Schedule to protect land reform laws.
• The Shankari Prasad ruling enabled the early Nehruvian state to implement land reforms without constitutional obstruction.

(b) Golak Nath v. State of Punjab

No Joint Sitting Provision for Constitutional Amendment Bills

solution.concept_anchor: No joint sitting for Constitution Amendment Bills — Rajya Sabha absolute veto
solution.strong_distractor: b — 'The President may summon a joint sitting of both Houses' sounds procedurally correct to students who know the President convenes joint sittings under Article 108 for ordinary bills and conflate that with the constitutional amendment context.
elimination_logic: Identify the nature of the bill: a Constitution Amendment Bill requiring special majority. This triggers a specific constitutional rule.
Article 108 (joint sitting) is explicitly NOT available for Constitution Amendment Bills — this is a firm constitutional rule. Eliminate option (b).

The bill did not fail on the floor of Lok Sabha — it was passed there. It was Rajya Sabha that declined. Rajya Sabha's equal and absolute power over constitutional amendments means the bill lapses. Eliminate options suggesting Lok Sabha can override.
Option (d) — the bill lapses and cannot be revived through joint sitting — is the only constitutionally accurate outcome.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap blends the joint sitting mechanism (applicable to ordinary bills) with constitutional amendment bills. Students who know that Presidential joint sittings resolve deadlocks assume the same mechanism applies universally. The critical constitutional distinction — that Article 108 explicitly excludes Constitution Amendment Bills — is not intuitive because students rarely ask 'does joint sitting apply here?' when they see a parliamentary deadlock scenario. The scenario is designed to trigger the joint sitting instinct before the student recalls the exclusion.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests one of the most consequential procedural distinctions in Indian parliamentary law — the absence of a joint sitting mechanism for constitutional amendments.

Applicable principle: Article 108, which empowers the President to summon a joint sitting of both Houses to resolve a legislative deadlock, explicitly does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills. When Rajya Sabha declines to pass such a bill (or passes it with amendments unacceptable to Lok Sabha), the bill lapses with no mechanism for revival.

Mapping to the scenario: Rajya Sabha's rejection (or non-passage with acceptable terms) of a Constitution Amendment Bill is a constitutional veto that cannot be overridden. Lok Sabha cannot invoke Article 108. The President has no relevant power here except to await a fresh bill.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Lok Sabha cannot proceed to pass the amendment unilaterally. Both Houses must independently pass with special majority.
• Option (b): Incorrect — the President cannot summon a joint sitting for Constitution Amendment Bills. Article 108 is inapplicable.
• Option (c): Incorrect — there is no constitutional provision for a mediation committee or conference committee for constitutional amendments (unlike in some other systems).
• Option (d): Correct — the bill lapses. Parliament may reintroduce the bill in a new session, but no shortcut exists to bypass Rajya Sabha's rejection.

Value Addition:
• This makes Rajya Sabha's veto power over constitutional amendments absolute — unlike Money Bills (where Rajya Sabha's role is merely recommendatory) or ordinary bills (where joint sitting can override).
• The constitutional design reflects that amendments to the fundamental law require broad consensus across both chambers.
• The only way forward after Rajya Sabha rejection is reintroduction — ideally after negotiating changes acceptable to Rajya Sabha.
